title: The three switches
desc: Three switches down here control three bulbs up there. Flip them as much as you like — but you only get to walk up once.
options: Flip one, go up, come back down, flip the next
Switch 1 on for ten minutes, off, switch 2 on, then go up
Turn all three on and see which lights first
Cannot be done in one trip
hints: One trip has to give you three separate facts.
A bulb has more than one state you can read. Light is only the obvious one.
Leave one on long enough to get hot, then switch it off before you climb.
good: You looked for a second signal instead of accepting the constraint as given.
improve: Name the rule out loud first: one trip means three distinguishable states, not two.
insight: Most impossible constraints are only impossible if you accept the variables you were handed.

title: First duplicate
desc: Return the first value that shows up twice. No sort, no lodash, no Set one-liner you half remember.
hints: What do you need to remember about the numbers already behind you?
You want a lookup that answers "seen this?" in constant time.
Walk once, keep a seen map, return the moment a lookup hits.
good: You wrote the loop instead of reaching for a one-liner you could not defend in an interview.
improve: Say the complexity out loud. If you cannot, you copied a shape rather than a solution.
insight: You can autocomplete a hash map. You cannot autocomplete knowing why it fits.

title: 40% more features
desc: "Teams that adopted our AI tool shipped 40% more features last quarter." What would you need to know before believing it? Name the strongest alternative explanation.
hints: Ask who ended up in the measured group, and how they got there.
Think about what makes a team adopt a new tool in the first place.
Fast teams adopt fast tools. The tool may be the symptom, not the cause.
good: You went after the sampling instead of arguing with the number.
improve: Name what evidence would change your mind. A critique nothing could satisfy is not a critique.
insight: "Compared to what?" is the cheapest question there is, and it defuses most statistics you will read this week.

title: Reverse it in place
desc: Two pointers, no built-in reverse, no copy.
hints: Two positions moving toward each other.
Swap, then move both inward. When do they stop?
While left < right: swap, then left++, right--.
good: You handled the stopping condition instead of guessing it.
improve: Trace it by hand on four items, then on five. Odd lengths are where off-by-ones live.
insight: Everyone knows this one until the day they write it with autocomplete off.

title: Explain a database index
desc: To someone who has never written code. One sentence, no jargon, and you may not compare it to the index of a book.
hints: Start from what the person wants: finding one thing among many.
Describe the outcome before the mechanism.
Something kept beside the data whose only job is making a search short instead of long.
good: You wrote it yourself, which is the part that builds the muscle.
improve: Cut one more word. Your first version is never the shortest available.
insight: If you cannot explain it without the stock analogy, you memorised the analogy, not the idea.

title: Find the heavy one
desc: Eight identical coins, one slightly heavier, a balance scale, exactly two weighings. Can you always find it?
options: No, three weighings minimum
Yes: 4 against 4, then 2 against 2, then 1 against 1
Yes: weigh 3 against 3 first, then narrow down
Only if you may weigh a coin against nothing
hints: Halving is the instinct. Count what halving actually costs you.
A balance has three outcomes, not two: left, right, level.
Three outcomes per weighing means splitting into three groups.
good: You noticed a balance gives three answers, so the useful split is in threes.
improve: Count the information each move buys before picking a strategy.
insight: Binary search is such a reflex that we apply it to tools that are not binary.

title: The turning triangle
desc: Two things are changing at the same time. Find both before you pick.

hints: Two rules run in parallel. Track them one at a time, not together.
The triangle does the same thing at every step. What is it?
A quarter turn each step, and the dot flips hollow to solid and back.
good: You separated the two rules instead of trying to see the whole pattern at once.
improve: Say each rule out loud before looking at the options. Options are designed to look plausible.
insight: When a pattern resists you, it usually has two rules stacked, not one complicated rule.

hook: This chart is lying to you.
title: Spot the trick
desc: Same data, honest numbers. So what makes the picture wrong?
figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 250 160" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart of two values, 10.0 and 10.4"><line x1="40" y1="14" x2="40" y2="126" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" opacity=".55"/><line x1="40" y1="126" x2="238" y2="126" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" opacity=".55"/><g font-size="9" font-family="JetBrains Mono, monospace" fill="currentColor" opacity=".6"><text x="34" y="129" text-anchor="end">9.8</text><text x="34" y="92" text-anchor="end">10.0</text><text x="34" y="55" text-anchor="end">10.2</text><text x="34" y="18" text-anchor="end">10.4</text></g><rect x="72" y="88" width="56" height="38" rx="3" fill="currentColor" opacity=".35"/><rect x="158" y="14" width="56" height="112" rx="3" fill="var(--accent)"/><g font-size="10" font-family="Instrument Sans, sans-serif" fill="currentColor"><text x="100" y="143" text-anchor="middle">2024</text><text x="186" y="143" text-anchor="middle">2025</text><text x="100" y="82" text-anchor="middle" opacity=".7">10.0</text><text x="186" y="8" text-anchor="middle" opacity=".7">10.4</text></g></svg>
options: The vertical axis starts at 9.8 instead of zero
Two years is not enough data to draw a chart
The bars should be lines, not rectangles
The colours make 2025 look more important
hints: Read the numbers on the left before you read the bars.
The second bar looks roughly three times the first. Is it?
A four percent difference is drawn as a triple-height bar. Where does the axis begin?
good: You checked the axis before trusting the shape. Most people never look at it.
improve: Next time say the real ratio out loud. Naming "4 percent, drawn as 300 percent" makes the trick impossible to unsee.
insight: You will see this exact chart in a real deck within a month. Probably one arguing for something you already want to believe.

hook: One of these breaks the rule.
title: The odd one out
desc: Five of the six follow the same rule. Find the one that does not.

B
C
D

hints: The rule connects the two halves of each tile.
Count something in the shape, then count the dots.
Corners and dots match everywhere except one.
good: You looked for a relationship between the parts instead of comparing tiles to each other.
improve: Check your rule against every tile before answering. A rule that fits four is not the rule.
insight: Spotting the odd one is easy. Stating the rule out loud is the part that transfers to real work.

title: Find the bug
desc: This average is slightly off, and sometimes returns NaN. Tap the line that causes it.
hints: The maths is fine. The problem is how many times the loop runs.
What is at index nums.length?
The comparison should stop one step earlier.
good: You went to the loop bounds first, which is where this class of bug always lives.
improve: Read the condition, not the body. The body looked innocent and it was.
insight: Off-by-one is the bug autocomplete writes most confidently, because it looks right.

hook: Call it twice. Watch it break.
title: The basket that remembers
desc: Calling add_item("apple") twice, in two unrelated places, returns a basket with two apples. Tap the line responsible.
hints: Nothing inside the function body is wrong.
When is the default value actually created?
The default list is built once, at definition time, and then shared by every call.
good: You looked at the signature instead of the body. Most people stare at append.
improve: Say when each line runs: at definition, or at call. That distinction catches a whole family of bugs.
insight: This one has been in the Python docs for twenty years and still ships to production every week.

title: Grouped by the wrong thing
desc: You wanted paid orders per customer. You got one row. Tap the line at fault.
hints: The filter is doing exactly what you asked.
What are you selecting per row, and what are you grouping by?
You group by the column you want one row for. That is not status.
good: You matched the grouping against the thing you selected, which is the check that catches this every time.
improve: Read a query in execution order, not written order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, then SELECT.
insight: A query that runs without error and answers a different question is worse than one that crashes.

hook: One door. Two guards. One lies.
title: The guarded door
desc: One door leads out, the other to a dead end. Two guards stand by them: one always tells the truth, one always lies, and you don't know which is which. You get one question, asked to one guard. What do you ask?
options: Which door leads out?
If I asked the other guard which door leads out, what would they say?
Are you the guard who tells the truth?
Is this the door that leads out?
hints: One question to one guard has to account for the one you didn't get to ask.
Ask about what the other guard would say, not what's actually true.
Whichever door they name, the real way out is the other one.
good: You built the answer around the guard you didn't get to ask, not just the one standing in front of you.
improve: Say out loud why the two errors — a lie about a lie, and a truth about a lie — end up pointing at the same wrong door.
insight: The liar's lie about a lie is the truth wearing a disguise.

hook: Twice as many sisters as brothers.
title: Count the siblings
desc: In one family, each girl has exactly as many sisters as brothers. Each boy has exactly twice as many sisters as brothers. How many children are in the family in total?
hints: Write two separate equations: one from a girl's point of view, one from a boy's.
A girl's sister-count is the total girls minus herself; her brother-count is just the total boys.
Solve girls - 1 = boys and girls = 2 * (boys - 1) together.
good: You wrote an equation for each point of view instead of guessing a number that felt about right.
improve: Plug your answer back into both original sentences and check each one holds, not just the algebra.
insight: Every siblings riddle is just two people describing the same family from different seats at the table.

title: Ask the missing question
desc: "9 out of 10 dentists recommend this toothpaste." What is the one question you would need answered before this claim means anything at all?
hints: Ask where the 10 dentists came from, not what they said.
A ratio depends entirely on who got asked, and how many people that really was.
Ask: how many dentists were surveyed in total, and how were they chosen?
good: You went straight for the sample instead of arguing with the ratio.
improve: Say the missing number out loud: 9 out of 10 could mean 900 out of 1,000 — or 9 out of 10 hand-picked people.
insight: A ratio without a sample size is a rumor wearing a lab coat.

hook: The total is always off by one item.
title: The off-by-one cart
desc: This should count every item in the cart, but it always misses the last one. Tap the line at fault.
hints: The loop body is fine. The problem is how many times it runs.
Count by hand for a cart with 3 items — how many times does count++ actually fire?
The "- 1" in the loop condition is cutting the last iteration short.
good: You traced how many times the loop actually runs instead of trusting that it looked right.
improve: When a count is off by exactly one, check the loop boundary first — it's the most common source.
insight: `< length - 1` and `<= length - 1` look one character apart and behave completely differently.

hook: It works once. Then it lies.
title: The cache that never updates
desc: This function is supposed to return a fresh total every time, but after the first call it always returns the same number. Tap the line responsible.
hints: The maths inside sum(amounts) is correct.
Ask: under what condition does this function actually recompute the total?
Once a user_id is cached, nothing here ever updates it again — even if amounts changes.
good: You looked past the arithmetic and asked when it actually runs, not just what it computes.
improve: A cache with no invalidation isn't a cache, it's a trap. Say out loud what should trigger a refresh.
insight: The bug isn't in the code that runs. It's in the code that stops running.

hook: Every customer shows the same total.
title: The join that multiplies
desc: You wanted total order value per customer. Every paid-in-instalments customer shows a suspiciously large number. Tap the line at fault.
lines: JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
hints: The maths (SUM) is doing exactly what it's told. The problem is what it's being told to sum over.
If one order has two payments, how many times does that order's row appear after the joins?
Joining payments duplicates every order paid in more than one instalment — before SUM ever runs.
good: You looked for row duplication before you looked at the arithmetic.
improve: Before trusting a SUM after a JOIN, ask: could this join make any row appear more than once?
insight: A JOIN that turns one row into three doesn't announce itself. The SUM just quietly triples.
